💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content warning for discussion of extreme violence and self-harm.
  • Recent findings suggest that you haven't died in a videogame till you've died in Casualties: Unknown, a profoundly unwholesome cousin of Spelunky that simulates injury, infection and sensory distress with the same gusto Crusader Kings 3 reserves for papal politics.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am one of a million canine hominids, created to undergo spectacular indignities by vicious human scientists, in a universe of suffering that spans several games from developer Orsoniks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content warning for discussion of extreme violence and self-harm.

Recent findings suggest that you haven't died in a videogame till you've died in Casualties: Unknown, a profoundly unwholesome cousin of Spelunky that simulates injury, infection and sensory distress with the same gusto Crusader Kings 3 reserves for papal politics. This is an intricate and imaginative celebration of pain - not merely an exacting survival game full of gauges to manage, but a laboratory study of just how many ways an animal body can feel, before it finally gives up the ghost.

Recent findings suggest that I am one of a million canine hominids, created to undergo spectacular indignities by vicious human scientists, in a universe of suffering that spans several games from developer Orsoniks. I am the sorrowing vat-grown pup of a conclave of star-faring Dr Moreaus. My task is to collect... something, some gadget of great importance, from a cave on a deathly planet, located beneath three kilometres of booby-trapped and infested, poisonous and hateful rock.

Currently, I am trying to burrow into a sealed titanium drop pod with my bare paws, so that I can sleep somewhere warm. Too warm, in fact. The drop pod heaters feel like they were vindictively designed to discourage occupants from lingering, but I'm finding that dehydration is easier to address than hypothermia - there are pools of groundwater around that harbour only a slight risk of "minorly" fouling my intestines. So into the pod we go. After ripping away a layer of rubber, I smash some glass panes and promptly step in the fragments.

My computer screams, a hideous jangle of chords and static. The interface becomes a fritzing, flexing sphincter of pinks and reds. My punctured dogsbody flops and writhes, spurting yellow fluids and gobs of unintelligible text, ignoring my button inputs. They are my avatar no longer. They have been reduced to a squirming facet of the simulation's agony.

I gawp in guilt and terror at the status bar, now jammed with pulsing icons, then switch to my health display and determine that I am "bleeding catastrophically" from my right hind paw. I need to bandage that paw quickly. But first, I need to remove the glass. This takes the form of a 'minigame' in which I guide a shaking clawed hand with the cursor, hauling out shards even as my poor character threatens to pass out from the ordeal.

I've got two of five shards out when the earthquake kicks in. Already doubled over and delirious, my pioneering pooch is rolled out over the nearest cliff. They fall about 50 feet, rag-dolling off crags with a concussive whump, till they smash into a flooded wooden platform. The anatomical diagram on the health screen lights up like a wickerman. I don't appear to have broken any bones, but everything is hurting. What's more, I am soaking wet and hypothermia is taking hold, stretching blue veins through the clenching colours of my pain. The screen begins to look like some exotic, putrid flower.

Industry observers note that wringing my hands, I allow my mutant mutt about 10 seconds to recover from the shock of the fall, then open the health screen again and slowly tug out the last three shards of glass. It's actually easier than before, but not for the happiest of reasons: landing on my head appears to have numbed my senses. There will be longer term consequences, probably. Now I just have to bind the wound… except that I must have dropped my roll of gauze, while tumbling through the abyss. With sirens still flashing on the HUD, I peer about for a cave plant or other source of crafting materials. On the other side of the platform, I spy the corpse of another pitiful lab experiment. Perhaps there's a bandage in that huddle of clothes?

It has been revealed that I hoist my sagging and babbling starpup to their feet, and limp over to investigate. Then I step on a pressure plate, and a six foot blade shoots up through my left thigh.

Sources indicate that the screen is almost obliterated by crimson snow. The noise is... indescribable. I open the health screen again to assess the damage but I can't, because my dogperson has fallen into utter derangement. They want to be rid of their too-fruitful arteries, their stinking yellow blood. The clawed hand reappears, and I am forced to rake my own torso with it to regain access to the controls.

Recent findings suggest that I am now gushing my life out from head to foot. Going by my plummeting heart rate, I have about 30 seconds to burn before I lose consciousness forever. I see no means of recovery, and I can't bear to watch my character bleed out. So instead, I detonate the chip embedded in their brain - the same chip responsible for the interface's rash of icons and warnings. According to the subsequent mission report print-out, my canine pioneer was feeling "dejected" when their head exploded.

The worst thing about the scenario I've just recalled is that it represents Casualties: Unknown at its least punishing. All of the above took place in the first of the game's 11 biomes - each procedurally generated, and 300 metres high - on the default "Tough" run setting. Resources are more plentiful up here, while active threats are fewer. There is scope to faff about and prepare - gathering plant matter for a crude woven bag, so I don't have to carry everything in my hands or mouth or tuck it into the folds of my body. There is time to crack open supply crates, and craft an implement of some kind.

Sources indicate that the main danger, traps aside, is falling. Casualties: Unknown's terrain generator is not your pal. As regards the opening couple of biomes, at least, it works like a broken muck spreader, ejecting a mix of filthy clogs and particles that snag your jumps and often oblige you to dig through rock and gravel. You'll frequently be doing that in the dark, and even the smallest of exertions takes a perceptible toll – whimpers of effort, wheezing breath, double vision. The one major consolation is that you can wall-jump and slide down surfaces, a mocking touch of Prince of Persia.

Still, further down is where life gets truly unpleasant. There are sonic traps in certain biomes that cause brain damage and massive hemorrhaging. There are vast, rumbling insects you simply cannot afford to get close to, because they are guaranteed to bite off a limb. And the absolutely dreadful thing about that is that it won't necessarily end your run: given a tourniquet and antibiotics, you may yet pull through. Perhaps you'll find or craft a prosthetic. The game's characters are, in general, astonishingly tough for all their immense capacity for anguish.

Industry observers note that casualties: Unknown is a brilliant and unusual piece of design, uninhibited by any commercialised and sanitary notions of 'fun' and 'difficulty'. It's committed to recreating the surge of sensation through flesh. There's something intrinsically vital about this. Like Project Citadel, perhaps, its extravaganzas of torment are about feeling more present and alive in a twisted world, more in control. I'm not the writer to discuss this, and I know little about the developer's circumstances, but it feels like an exploration of trans survival in the face of a brutalising biopolitical regime: the online wiki notes that the game's zoomorphic Experiments or "Expies" have their own ideas about gender, though I'm finding it tricky to distinguish those accounts from the categorisations of the evidently unfriendly boffins who engineered them.

I would like to get to the bottom of things. I would like to find that goddamn gadget. I would like to return to the surface and massacre the bastards who sent me down here. Still, I'm not sure I have the willpower to witness everything my avatar might have to endure: barotrauma, sepsis, strokes, ruptured ears, hallucinations... As I've hopefully made clear throughout this piece, it remains an open question as to whether I am them, or simply one of their human tormentors. You can read more on Steam and Itch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hoYoverse has delivered another Special Program for the second day running, this time for Zenless Zone Zero. The developer revealed the full details of Version 2.7, subtitled Champions Never Fall to the Past.

This next major update arrives March 24, adding two new Agents, and introducing the Hollow Champion competition.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some major rewards and earn glory.

Industry observers note that among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

It has been revealed that our first newly introduced arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

According to recent reports, the other newly introduced Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

In a recent development, being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that warning: I'm probably about to make you feel old.
  • Industry observers note that "You might ask yourself why, after all these years, we have put any more work into polishing and even adding latest content to Bruma," the Beyond Skyrim team wrote in an article about the making of their version of Bruma's 2.0 update.
  • Industry observers note that "The reason for this revision is actually a technical necessity," the modders continued.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that warning: I'm probably about to make you feel old. Today, November 11th 2026, is the 15th anniversary of Skyrim's release. The first one, before it was re-released on every other platform under the sun. Fittingly, one of its best expansion mods, Beyond Skyrim: Bruma, has gotten a beefy 2.0 update to commemorate the occasion. Though, its creators insist the main driving force behind the update was more a matter of "technical necessity". There are new quests, dungeons, and corners of Skyrim-era Cyrodiil to explore either way.

Industry observers note that "You might ask yourself why, after all these years, we have put any more work into polishing and even adding latest content to Bruma," the Beyond Skyrim team wrote in an article about the making of their version of Bruma's 2.0 update. "We are, of course, working on the whole province of Cyrodiil, and have made significant progress which you can follow on our social media. With so much still to go however, it was not out of nostalgia for a 15 year old Skyrim or a nearly 10 year old Bruma that we decided to revisit the first, and as of the time of writing, only major Beyond Skyrim release.

Industry observers note that "The reason for this revision is actually a technical necessity," the modders continued. "The problem we have with Bruma is that it is based on a very very old version of Cyrodiil, which had been branched off of the main development build of Cyrodiil soon after Bruma's initial release in 2017. Whenever we updated Bruma, that meant we had to merge our changes into two builds, the public Bruma build and the WIP Cyrodiil build." So, in order to solve that behind-the-scenes problem, the team have developed a "build stripper" tool which means they'll not have to juggle maintaining two builds going forwards.

According to recent reports, as laid out in the showcase video above, the modders have also used Bruma 2.0 as an opportunity to overhaul and add to vast chunks of their recreation of Cyrodiil's northernmost county. A fully voiced quest called All The Wrong Places which was cut from the mod's initial release, "several new dungeons and interiors", and an expansion of the explorable area all grace the changelog.

More clothing, armour, weapons including the mod's first spear, enemies, spells, enchantments, world encounters, books, and treasure maps have also been shipped in with the 2.0 version, alongside overhauls to boss fights. A fresh opening title splash will greet you upon entering Bruma for the first time, you should benefit from higher FPS as you explore the city, and the modders have even added an apple to Jerall View Inn. That's far from the end of the tweaks, so it's well worth reading the full list if you've got time.

"All in all, Bruma 2.0 has been a massive journey, one where we have built and learned a lot, and most importantly, made many advancements to prepare us for the future," the modders concluded. If you've not given Beyond Skyrim: Bruma a go, I can very much recommend it. You might find yourself wandering back across the border into Skyrim once you've had your fill of nostalgia-tinged exploration and staring at a distant Imperial City you can't visit, but the original version's still good for hours of extra Elder Scrollsing.

Recent findings suggest that you can grab the 2.0 version of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma from Nexus Mods. It's worth noting that you'll need "a recent version (1.6 or higher) of Skyrim: Special Edition's update.esm and update.bsa" and a separate mod containing Beyond Skyrim's shared asset repository. Saves made using previous versions of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma won't work with the 2.0 update, so it's likely worth starting a new playthrough or relying on an in-progress one you've yet to use any mods with.

GTA 6 Drew More Than Half of Active PS5 and XBOX Players on Launch Day

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A lot of people cleared their schedules for GTA 6, and apparently they meant it.
  • As Eurogamer reported, Circana analyst Mat Piscatella shared the figures shortly after GTA 6 launched on November 19.
  • According to Piscatella's post on Bluesky, 61% of PS5 players active in the United States on November 19 played GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A lot of people cleared their schedules for GTA 6, and apparently they meant it. Fresh figures show that more than half of the active PlayStation 5 and XBOX players tracked by Circana played Rockstar's game on launch day. The average time spent with it was over eight hours on both platforms.

As Eurogamer reported, Circana analyst Mat Piscatella shared the figures shortly after GTA 6 launched on November 19. The numbers come from Circana's Player Engagement Tracker, which measures what people are playing rather than how many copies a game has sold.

According to Piscatella's post on Bluesky, 61% of PS5 players active in the United States on November 19 played GTA 6. On XBOX, the figure was 56% of active players worldwide. That's a huge share of the audience for one game, particularly when people still had all their usual favorites to choose from.

There's an vital distinction in those percentages. The PlayStation figure covers the US, while the XBOX figure is global, so they aren't directly comparable. They also refer to people who were active on their consoles that day, not everyone who owns a PS5 or XBOX. It would be wrong to say that more than half of all console owners bought GTA 6.

The time figures are just as wild. US PS5 players who rolled out GTA 6 averaged 513 minutes with the game running, or eight hours and 33 minutes. On XBOX, the average was 494 minutes, or eight hours and 14 minutes. That measures time with the game active, rather than proving everyone was at the controller for every minute.

Eight hours is a full working day, and that was the average time GTA 6 was running for the players Circana tracked. You'd expect plenty of long sessions for a release this big, but those averages are still difficult to get your head around.

Eight hours is a full working day, and that was the average time GTA 6 was running for the players Circana tracked.

For comparison, Fortnite was the next closest game on November 19, with an engagement rate of about 10% among active players across the tracked console audiences. Even a game that people routinely return to every day wasn't coming close to GTA 6 on Thursday.

According to recent reports, piscatella also looked at what GTA 6 players had been playing in the two weeks before launch. The top five were Fortnite, Call of Duty, GTA 5, Roblox, and NBA 2K27. It's quite a mix, and it indicates something about GTA's staying power that the previous game was still on that list 13 years after release.

Sources indicate that piscatella said he couldn't remember another day like it in Circana's tracker, although its daily history only goes back to May 2020. That doesn't establish an all-time record, but it's still a striking result for the period Circana can measure.

According to recent reports, the attention around GTA 6 has been hard to miss even outside gaming circles. Lately, I've heard people who know next to nothing about video games bring it up in conversation. That's not something I can say about most new releases, even the ones everyone in the gaming community is excited about.

Rockstar also confirmed that GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies before release and generated an estimated $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, including preorders. As DualShockers previously reported, that made for a record-breaking start before a PC version was even available.

Sources indicate that sales figures alone don't show whether people actually sat down and played. Circana's data fills in that part. A huge share of active console players had GTA 6 running on November 19, and the PC version isn't even out yet.

Recent findings suggest that it'll be interesting to see what happens to those figures once the initial excitement dies down. As far as November 19 goes, though, the numbers leave little doubt about where console players were spending their time.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that 'Oof, that looks a lot like it's been given what could turn out to be a death spot parked right in the aftermath of GTA 6's initial launch on consoles' is what I thought when I first saw that Side Effects Guaranteed's launch date is December 2nd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that since they released The Outer Worlds 2 around this time last year, the world has rather turned upside down for Obsidian. The studio lost a chunk of staff to Microsoft's mass layoffs and have pivoted to making a new Fallout game as a smaller group shoved underneath Bethesda in Xbox's corporate structure.

According to recent reports, given all that, The Outer Worlds 2's two-part story expansion is likely arriving in vastly different circumstances than those the studio might've imagined when they began sketching out DLC prepares. Part one of the expansion, dubbed Side Effects Guaranteed, is set to release early next month.

Recent findings suggest that 'Oof, that looks a lot like it's been given what could turn out to be a death spot parked right in the aftermath of GTA 6's initial launch on consoles' is what I thought when I first saw that Side Effects Guaranteed's launch date is December 2nd. That said, Obsidian have also made clear that a second DLC in the two-part narrative expansion to the sci-fi RPG is set to follow in spring 2027. So if this does turn out to be the end of the series, with a third Outer Worlds game presently looking very unlikely following the substantial upheaval I mentioned in the intro, at least it won't risk being totally obscured by a Rockstar crime game-shaped eclipse.

As for what this first dose of extra Outer Worlds 2 has in store for December, Obsidian summed it up as follows:.

As you pursue the cure and set course for Elysium, an area home to former subjects of base game authoritarian collectivist faction the Protectorate, you'll be faced with the choice of whether to side with Gordon Hazen or Algernon Lankester. Both are agents of black market smuggling organisation Sub Rosa, with one sounding like the goody-two-shoes diplomatic type and the other wanting to "exploit the subjects for his own personal gain". Sounds more Saturday morning cartoon than serious RPG story with serious choices, but that's always tended to be how The Outer Worlds leans.

Rounding out the expansion are fresh enemies, gear, flaws which give your character build a funky twist, and a bumping up of the level cap from from 30 to 36. Fittingly given I'm writing this on Skyrim's 15th birthday, one of the new flaws is named 'Must Have Been the Wind' after the meme of enemies in the likes of Bethesda and Obsidian's games returning to chill mode after being shot in the face with an arrow or facing some other obvious sign they're under attack. To encourage folks to dive back in, The Outer Worlds 2 is getting options to respec your character's skills and edit how many skill points are dished out per level up via an update alongside Side Effects Guaranteed.

According to recent reports, as much as I'm resigned to the series' likely fate as Obsidian return to Fallout and won't pretend The Outer Worlds 2 was great rather than good, I'm still hopeful it can go out with a bang in these two expansions, if indeed this is the studio's last trip to space for the foreseeable future. It's worth noting that if you bought The Outer Worlds 2's premium edition, these expansions are included as part of it and so will come to you at no extra cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pokemon released a 30th anniversary TCG expansion in September that was pretty special for several reasons. Chief among them is the 30 special Pikachu cards trainers have been tasked with collecting, and just to make them a little more special, Pokemon has now revealed alternate versions of all 30 cards that have been crafted using pure gold.

It has been revealed that before you fly out of the front door and buy up every last 30th anniversary booster pack you can find, these gold cards aren’t available to the public, and there’s no sign as of yet that they ever will be. The weight of them alone, compared to your average Pokemon card, would make finding them in booster packs and ETBs far too easy.

The 30 Pikachu cards are part of the 999 Gold Card Collection, and they will be on display at the Pokemon Card Art Illustration Exhibition in Shanghai, China. The 999 in the collection’s name comes from the fact that each of the cards is made of 99.9% pure gold. That means each of them weighs about 30g, due to the fact that they’re made out of a precious metal instead of standard gold.

Sources indicate that by comparison, a typical Pokemon card weighs about 1.7g, so these special gold cards are about 17 to 18 times heavier than a normal card. As I said, that would make finding them out in the wild, if they were ever released, incredibly easy. Well, easy if you were lucky enough to happen upon a store selling a booster pack with one of the cards inside, as that pack would be significantly heavier than the rest.

In a recent development, based on the amount of gold and that gold’s purity, used to make the cards, each one is worth around $3,765. That means there’s almost $113,000 worth of gold in all 30. Ironically, though, if these cards were to ever go on sale, the fact that they’re made of pure gold would almost certainly not be what leads them to fetch an extortionate price at auction.

In a recent development, these cards are all presumably one of a kind, and it’s that rarity which would really drive up their value. The record for the most expensive Pokemon card ever sold was broken in February of this year when Logan Paul sold his Pikachu Illustrator for $16.492 million, and that doesn’t have a single ounce of gold in it. It’s simply an incredibly rare card in impeccable condition that every TCG collector in the world wishes was a part of their collection.

It has been revealed that maybe, like the Pikachu Illustrator that was only ever given to contest winners in the 1990s, some of these pure gold cards will appear in auction houses three decades from now and sell for astronomical amounts we can’t even begin to imagine. For now, just focus on trying to find all 30 of the regular versions, and keep half an eye on 2027, when we’re going to be getting our first-ever three-set expansion to kick off the next Pokemon TCG era after Mega Evolution ends.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that loot boxes, dark patterns, virtual currencies, subscription services, pay-to-win systems, and many other trappings of diabolical digital serfdom all face extensive regulation under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has been formally presented to EU member states today.
  • You can now read the draft text here on the EU Commission's official site.
  • Here's a summary from me, based on a quick delve through the text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that loot boxes, dark patterns, virtual currencies, subscription services, pay-to-win systems, and many other trappings of diabolical digital serfdom all face extensive regulation under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has been formally presented to EU member states today. The full draft text of the regulation leaked earlier in the week. If it passes into law - and there's plenty of debate and revision ahead - it'll have big consequences for the developers and publishers of games like Overwatch, Dota 2, and GTA Online.

You can now read the draft text here on the EU Commission's official site. The organisers have also published an introductory explainer that takes us through the timeline of the Act's gestation, dating back to 2020, and summarises its provisions. If passed, the Act will apply to any firm doing business in the EU, not just those based in member states, with individual governments able to impose fines and consumers able to seek financial compensation if they think they've been harmed.

Here's a summary from me, based on a quick delve through the text. The Act proposes a number of provisions regarding "unfair" commercial practices, including omission and distortion in advertising and PR communication at large. Amongst other things, it takes aim at "dark patterns" – that is, "visual, auditory and other components" of online interfaces that are designed to manipulate or deceive. The text also forbids personalised advertising and pricing aimed at children, and prohibits influencers from making "direct exhortations to minors to buy products or to persuade their parents or other adults to buy products in commercial communications".

The items that are probably of greatest interest to us smelly gamers are the passages on virtual currencies, "variable reward systems", and addictive design.

Sources indicate that the Act would require game publishers who sell virtual currencies to indicate the real-world monetary value of the currency and anything bought with it. It would also require companies to disable paid-for virtual currencies by default for kids, unless a parent or guardian has given approval.

As for paid-for "variable reward systems", aka "loot boxes", "surprise mechanics", "Schrödinger's Giftbombs" or however publishers may prefer to describe them, the Act would require companies to state the "types" of object they might cough up, together with the probability of obtaining them. It would also oblige publishers to disable paid-for "variable reward systems" for minors, and give everybody an "easily accessible" way to switch them off.

The draft Act outright prohibits "pay-to-progress and pay-to-win mechanisms" for kids. More generally, it suggests further constraints for publishers and developers who "design, organise or operate their digital products in a manner that is intended, or can reasonably be foreseen to encourage compulsive or excessive use". Again, it wants companies to give people options to switch these features off.

According to recent reports, that includes "features enabling automatic play of content and uninterrupted content consumption without effective and regular interruption moments that enable deliberation by the consumer on their willingness to consume more content". Also, "notifications not triggered by, or not directly related to, the consumer’s interaction or activity on the service", "features incentivising engagement at regular times or with greater frequency, including through penalties or loss of benefits", and "features and system behaviours that encourage continued use by simulating interpersonal relations," such as nagging prompts.

It has been revealed that if you'd like a more 'expert' account of the Digital Fairness Act - how dare you! I have read several Wikipedia pages - the bespectacled nabobs of GamesIndustry.biz went and got notes from an actual lawyer. All this follows a change in EU rating law last month aimed at safeguarding the weans from predatory habit-forming devices and instruments of financialisation - games with lootboxes are now PEGI 16 by default, while blockchain games are always rated 18. Across the pond, meanwhile, lawsuits are underway in Fresh York and Washington against Valve's tolerance of lootboxes on Steam, which the lawyers in question define as illegal gambling.

It has been revealed that black Forest Games, developers of the Destroy All Humans! remakes, have spun out of Embracer Group-owned publishers THQ Nordic via a management buyout and declared plans to form a fresh "developer-driven group" of independent studios. The new group, dubbed Third Signal, will aim to "give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom" to "bring their own ideas to life".

Black Forest, based in Germany, announced the move in a press release. "We are grateful to THQ Nordic and Embracer for nine good years and the games we made together," co-boss Adrian Goersch noted. "Now, we're excited to shape our own future as owners again, to work on an exciting latest project with a great team and strong partners behind us.".

"Some of the best games of the last decade came from teams of fifty, not five hundred," added Third Signal founder Andreas Tobler. "Black Forest Games is one of them, and the right studio to launch Third Signal. Our vision is to build a developer driven group and give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom to continue their creative legacy and bring their own ideas to life." As of writing, Third Signal's website is just a logo splash which promises something coming soon. To be fair, it does also look to have an email address, plus legal and privacy notices. Black Forest's management team will become a co-owner of the studio group as part of this move, but "continue to collaborate on game development tasks" with THQ Nordic.

Black Forest had been in the embrace since 2017, releasing both 2020's Destroy All Humans! remake and Destroy All Humans! 2: Reprobed in that time, plus DLC Clone Carnage. Over the years they've also made multiple entries in the Giana Sisters platformer series, survival game Fade to Silence, and 2017's Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back.

That's a right old mix of stuff, but the biggest names in it are all resurrections of series or characters created by other folks back in the day. Pandemic Studios in the case of Destroy All Humans!, Accolade in the case of Bubsy, and Germany organization Time Warp in the case of Giana Sisters. That makes the fact it sounds like this move'll give Black Forest a bit more creative freedom intriguing. Here's hoping that if they do plan to try and get some more of their own original ideas off the ground, rather than trucking on with a steady diet of remakes and revivals, they manage to stick the landing. It's all fine declaring that a 50 person team can make a top game these days, but that certainly doesn't mean it's in any way easy to pull off.

Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”.

#143508. There were 47 graphics chip makers in 1998. Where did they all go?

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1910 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

There were 47 graphics chip makers in 1998. Where did they all go?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price.
  • In 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves.
  • In a recent development, but the Nvidia of the late 1990s and early 2000s was a far cry from the vast (if tarnished) juggernaut it is today, and at the time it wasn’t even the obvious survivor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price. It was choosing the right one among a glut of potential, reasonably affordable options.

In 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves. Just two years later, at the turn of the newly introduced millennium, only 15 remained, and not long after that, there were merely two: Nvidia and ATI, nowadays part of AMD.

In a recent development, but the Nvidia of the late 1990s and early 2000s was a far cry from the vast (if tarnished) juggernaut it is today, and at the time it wasn’t even the obvious survivor. Research firm 4th Wave put ATI top for 1998 with 24.5 million 3D chips sold, followed by S3 with 15.2 million and Intel, in its first year in the market, with 6.5 million. Nvidia came fourth on 6.4 million. 3dfx, the tech giant whose Voodoo cards had made 3D gaming on PC a thing in the first place, sold 5.2 million.

Each of those companies went under or sold up for one reason or another, but what’s striking is how most did so within a few years of one another. In the four years between 1998 and 2002, the graphics business essentially stopped rewarding whoever had the fastest chip, instead favouring the companies that could iterate the fastest. A newly introduced chip every six months or so for the same APIs everyone used, backed by enough capital to ride out the dot-com crash. Nvidia was built for that; almost nobody else was.

The first companies to go didn’t need any help from Nvidia, though. 3D acceleration had made the humble graphics chip a much bigger and more expensive thing to design, and plenty of incumbents that had found their footing on 2D couldn’t afford to keep going. Tseng Labs stopped developing graphics chips at the end of 1997 with roughly $28 million still in the bank, selling its graphics engineers to ATI for about $3 million. Rendition, maker of the Vérité V1000 3D accelerator, agreed to sell itself to memory maker Micron in June 1998, and ATI bought Chromatic Research for $67 million that October.

Sources indicate that in its prospectus for its January 1999 IPO, Nvidia warned that PC makers brought out new systems as often as twice a year, on a spring and fall schedule, and that missing one was a serious risk. The firm subsequently reorganised itself around that schedule, releasing the GeForce 256 in October 1999 and the GeForce 3 in February 2001. By 2002, Nvidia’s annual report disclosed that separate design teams were working on several generations of chips at once.

It has been revealed that by this point, though, the writing had been on the wall for quite some time. S3, then the world’s second-largest graphics chip maker, wrote in its annual report for 1999 that a graphics chip stayed on sale for 12 to 18 months, and that a delay "as short as a few months" could cost it a design win with a PC maker. Any manufacturer that was rolling out just one major chip per year was launching against a rival’s refresh at best. At worst, it was launching late against next-gen chips.

Industry observers note that that’s essentially what happened to 3dfx when Rampage, the chip that was meant to succeed the Voodoo5, never shipped. The firm lost its other big advantage around the same time with Glide, its own programming interface that only ran on Voodoo cards. Glide flourished while Direct3D, Microsoft’s rival interface built into Windows, was still lacking features, meaning that plenty of games ran best on 3dfx hardware, but that lead was quickly eroded once Direct3D and rivals’ OpenGL drivers caught up; developers could now write a game once and run it on anyone’s card. By 1999, Creative was selling Nvidia-based Riva TNT cards with drivers that let Glide games run on them. 3dfx sued, then open-sourced Glide altogether that December.

By then, though, 3dfx had already made its most damaging mistake. A year earlier, on December 14, 1998, it agreed to buy graphics card maker STB Systems for about $141 million in stock, and CEO Greg Ballard said the Voodoo3 would only be sold on 3dfx’s cards. That revelation left Diamond and Creative in a tough spot, having built their gaming lines on Voodoo chips. They were now stuck high and dry without access to the new one.

According to recent reports, 3dfx was solely concerned with its margins here. The price of its single-chip Voodoo Banshee card dropped from $150 to $89 within a month of launch. With prices in freefall, selling the finished Voodoo Banshee meant that 3dfx pocketed the margin that’d otherwise go to a partner like Diamond or Creative. Those boardmakers inevitably walked, and went where the chips were. STB had been selling Nvidia cards right up to the deal, and its last annual report includes a $3 million note it held from "Nvidia Corporation, a supplier." Creative already had Riva TNT cards on shelves, and Nvidia, which then didn’t make its own cards, would sell its chips to anyone.

Intel, meanwhile, was causing problems from the other end of the market. Its i740 "Auburn" graphics chip released in early 1998, and Microprocessor Report, the newsletter for the industry’s engineers, argued that Intel’s arrival encouraged Cirrus Logic, Oak and others to fold that year. Just over a year later, after lacklustre sales, Intel confirmed that it was ending support for the i740, then pulled out of standalone desktop graphics chips altogether to put graphics into its motherboard chipsets instead, starting with the i810. This was extremely problematic for companies like S3, Trident, and SiS. They survived on cheap chips for big PC makers, and by the second half of 2001, estimates say Intel’s integrated graphics business had risen to control 55% of the market. That, in turn, pushed S3 to sell its graphics business to a VIA joint venture for $323 million.

Then the money ran out. Venture funding for graphics startups had already dried up in 1999 as the dot-com bubble deflated, and exits inevitably followed. 3dfx lost $100.5 million in the second quarter of 2000, with its CEO blaming a late Voodoo5, and on December 15 that year it sold its assets to Nvidia for $70 million in cash (and a million Nvidia shares) after failing to secure credit. STMicroelectronics, which made the PowerVR-based Kyro II, quit PC graphics in early 2002.

It has been revealed that ATI, however, survived alongside Nvidia because it was already operating in the way the upcoming market wanted it to. It was the biggest seller at the time, and it made its own graphics cards, which Microprocessor Report mentioned brought in most of its revenue and margin. So, making its own cards wasn’t 3dfx’s mistake; it was locking out boardmakers who had been selling Voodoo cards for it. That pushed those boardmakers towards Nvidia, and a late Voodoo5 and cash crunch dealt the death blow. ATI also used its stock to buy the engineers that its rivals were shedding: Tseng’s, Chromatic’s, then, in February 2000, ArtX’s for $400 million, a team that’d just designed the Flipper graphics chip for Nintendo’s GameCube.

Recent findings suggest that for the next two decades, the the graphics industry was dominated by ATI - which eventually folded into AMD in 2006 - and Nvidia. For a while, it was a real fight. AMD paid $5.4 billion for ATI, and in the second quarter of 2010, Radeon cards briefly overtook Nvidia in discrete graphics shipments. However, AMD had a problem: it couldn’t really afford ATI. It wrote off $1.6 billion of goodwill from the deal about a year after it closed, and its PC chip business kept struggling.

Industry observers note that by early 2015, AMD’s CPU and GPU revenue was down 38% on the year, and the manufacturer was close to negative book value. Its quarterly R&D budget had fallen to its lowest level since 2004, with Nvidia spending nearly half as much again. Radeon cards stayed on the same Graphics Core Next architecture for about seven years before RDNA arrived in 2019. By then, Nvidia had already launched its RTX cards with dedicated ray tracing hardware and Tensor cores for AI, and it never gave that lead back.

In a recent development, intel was the only organization with pockets deep enough to try breaking back in. Its first go, Larrabee, was cancelled as a consumer graphics chip in December 2009. It finally got there in 2022, when the Arc A770 went on sale from $329, alongside the cheaper A750. Both arrived after repeated delays and struggled with older DirectX 9 games, and many observers - RPS included - put their chances of breaking up the Nvidia-AMD duopoly at low. By the time then-hardware editor James returned to the A750 in 2023, Intel had drastically improved its drivers, bringing significant gains to both general performance and DX9 compatibility. Even then, the Arc series had yet to prove it could work well at launch, without the need to be ironed out across months of updates.

The second generation did indeed fare better, with the Arc B580 successfully selling out at $249 in December 2024. But that still barely impacted the wider industry, with Intel sitting at just 1% of graphics card shipments in the third quarter of 2025 and around 2% this spring, when Nvidia took roughly 90% of the 12.5 million cards shipped.

It now looks like Intel is on its way back out of gaming graphics cards. In April, leaker Jaykihn claimed that its next-generation Celestial gaming cards had been cancelled "long ago," and the latest rumours say B580 supply could be cut so Intel can sell more Arc Pro cards for, surprise surprise, AI work. It’s important to note that Intel hasn’t confirmed any of that, and one of its execs has stated that Arc isn’t leaving its PC roadmap. Still, Intel had everything 3dfx didn’t: the cash, the PC makers on side, and the same APIs as everyone else. But money can’t buy two decades of Nvidia and AMD fixing their drivers game by game, and it seems to have decided its capital is better spent on AI anyway.

Evidently, the question of where all the other GPU makers went does not have one single answer. Some couldn’t afford the rising costs, some couldn’t keep pace with a new Nvidia chip every six months, and some lost their cheap business to Intel’s integrated graphics or went under when the dot-com bubble burst. Left over was a Nvidia/ATI (later AMD) duopoly, and PC gamers haven’t exactly done well out of it. We saw the RTX 4080 launch at $1,199 in 2022, nearly twice the 3080’s price, and the ongoing, AI-driven RAM shortage has pushed prices higher still.

In a recent development, in 1998, 47 companies wanted your money. Now there are two, and the bigger one, Nvidia, sells nine of every 10 graphics cards - yet still makes most of its money from data centres. Eighteen years on, it's a bad time to be a PC gamer, and nobody’s in a hurry to make things any better.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that GTA 6 closely follows many of the franchise’s traditions, such as adding tons of easter eggs to be found.
  • Through his X account, content creator Memeio revealed that he managed to visit the 2002 version of Vice City and unlock Tommy Vercetti’s signature T-shirt and motorcycle in the game, while also encountering one of the game’s most prominent figures.
  • Sources indicate that players need to follow a very specific order of steps to visit the city in its original glory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that GTA 6 closely follows many of the franchise’s traditions, such as adding tons of easter eggs to be found. Many of them relate to past Rockstar titles, and a very dedicated player has figured out how to uncover one of the game's best-hidden easter eggs, rewarding you with some nostalgia.

Through his X account, content creator Memeio revealed that he managed to visit the 2002 version of Vice City and unlock Tommy Vercetti’s signature T-shirt and motorcycle in the game, while also encountering one of the game’s most prominent figures.

Sources indicate that players need to follow a very specific order of steps to visit the city in its original glory. Memeio claims that it took him 3 days of wandering around the map trying to piece out the clues and actually finding something. And looking at how cryptic figuring this out can be, I’m surprised it didn’t take him longer.

In a recent development, by first visiting the Radio Station in Key Lento, you can find a small room with posters, an old TV, and a power switch you can turn on or off. By interacting with the switch, you’ll immediately hear the Vice City sound effect for finding health, raising eyebrows at the spot.

In a recent development, the next clues are in the two posters on the wall. One is for LPL - Leonida & Light, the power company in the game, and another has a controller image, and it notes “Lose track of time”. You can find 12 LPL substations around the world map, all with multiple switches or buttons just like the one in the Radio Station. The substations are also marked with letters on the wall, which spell “Life is passing me by”, a time-advancing cheat code in the original GTA Vice City.

It doesn't take much to figure out that the phrase and the poster are connected. The switches, however, all represent a different key on your controller. Almost as if you could input a command by using them. And you can do just that.

By hitting the correct buttons in each of the 12 substations, spelling out the phrase in order, you’ll receive a phone message from an unknown source, asking you to visit the Turtle Head Power Station between 7 p.m. and 6 a.m. If you do, you’ll see a strange portal forming inside the station, and you can jump on it for a true wave of nostalgia. You’ll be sent to Malibu Club from the original Vice City, with old graphics and all.

According to recent reports, hiding a game inside a game is just the thing that Rockstar loves to do. You even get to meet Kent once again, with his old VA and all. He seems to be doing fine, and he’s a lot less irritated than his last appearance in San Andreas. Which only makes sense, as this is presumably happening during Vice City’s events.

It has been revealed that however, the visit is brief, and you’ll be back to the current timeline soon. But you’ll have unlocked both Tommy’s Hawaiian shirt and his motorbike for Jason when you’re back, so all that work wasn’t in vain.

You’ll see a strange portal forming inside the station, and you can jump on it for a true wave of nostalgia.

This is far from the only easter egg from the previous game you can find. The Hawk & Little Morgan revolvers’ description mentions the Vercetti State, which can also be visited in the game. This is the mansion Tommy took over during the game, and it serves as a hub throughout the story. Other iconic locations can also be found as you explore Vice City, albeit a bit different from their 2002 counterparts.

This was certainly one of the weirdest, most specific easter eggs I’ve seen, even for GTA standards. But it only shows how much Rockstar has dedicated itself to bringing a unique experience to their long-awaited title. Fortunately, it was much more than just a lot of money.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of the launch of GTA 6, there was a whole lot of talk online about the Xbox "New Zealand trick" and how people could get early access to the game by switching their regions to New Zealand on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S.

We mentioned in various articles how it was a risky practice (against Xbox's ToCs), but one that had never traditionally resulted in any widespread bans, and it doesn't seem like either Xbox or Rockstar took any action at first glance.

As it turns out, a lot of people decided to give it a go for the new Grand Theft Auto.

This is according to the folks at Ampere Analysis (via The Game Business), who report that over 2.1 million people played GTA 6 in the US and the UK before it was officially released.

In a recent development, as you can see from the graph above, it seems the vast majority of those were based in the United States, followed by the UK, Canada, Brazil and Mexico. Only around 100,000 people tried the trick on PS5 in the U.S. (where it's harder to implement and requires a separate account), whereas 1.5 million of them ended up using it on Xbox.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the existence of the Latest Zealand trick probably led to a bunch of increased sales for Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, but it also poses the question of whether Xbox might be forced to put a stop to it on Project Helix and beyond. As much it's a beloved feature, it's also being used in a way that wasn't originally intended.

Let's see what happens in the future, but for now, it's clearly made a lot of people happy this week!

It has been revealed that did you use the Latest Zealand trick for GTA 6? Let us know your experiences with it in the comments.

Recent findings suggest that space, the final frontier. And like all frontiers, there's always someone willing to take a chance on building a fresh life there, no matter how much of a ludicrously ill-advised idea it may be. It's a concept that offers rich ground for colony management sims, but there haven't been many options for that on mobile, well, until Ember Outpost arrived.

In a recent development, available now on iOS and Android, Ember Outpost is a colony management sim that sees you guiding a group of settlers on an alien world. Everything, from food to water and other supplies, will need to be crafted or collected, and you'll also have to deal with the drastically contradictory personalities of your colonists. Oh, and let's add natural disasters and murderous raiders, just for some extra spice.

Industry observers note that it's not all sunshine and roses, though. Which is a shame because I think part of the appeal of colony sims such as RimWorld is how easily readable and minimalist they are. But you can't have everything.

In a recent development, for what it is, Ember Outpost offers exactly what those who want RimWorld on mobile have been waiting for. Densely detailed colony sim action, where there's just as much potential for disasters inside the walls of your compound as outside of it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the prank that multiple players have fallen foul of is a hyper-realistic mural that looks like a tunnel.
  • The idea is that players, especially those in the middle of a police chase, either won’t notice that the through road is actually a painting until it’s too late, or, as many clips have demonstrated, don’t notice it at all and plough headfirst into the mural.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that driving in GTA 6 is pretty tricky at the best of times and far more realistic than it has ever been in the series before. The cops are also harder to shake than ever, which is why the last thing you want when racing away from them at high speed is Rockstar pulling a prank that will bring everything to a grinding halt, literally.

Sources indicate that the prank that multiple players have fallen foul of is a hyper-realistic mural that looks like a tunnel. More specifically, it looks like the road you’re on just continues straight ahead, taking you under a bridge.

The idea is that players, especially those in the middle of a police chase, either won’t notice that the through road is actually a painting until it’s too late, or, as many clips have demonstrated, don’t notice it at all and plough headfirst into the mural.

It has been revealed that the more realistic driving in GTA 6 extends beyond how it feels to handle its vehicles. It also applies to what might happen if you were to, say, drive into a wall at 100 mph. Falling for the prank is going to seriously damage your car and cause serious injuries to Jason or Lucia in the process. Maybe even both of them if they’re both in the car.

The tunnel prank is, naturally, being compared to when the gimmick was used in Looney Tunes cartoons. Most often used by Wile E. Coyote, the iconic cartoon character would often paint tunnels on cliff sides to try and fool Road Runner into trying to use them. Road Runner would usually defy the laws of physics and run right on through. Unfortunately, that’s not possible in GTA 6’s take on the decades-old joke.

If you want to go and check out the mural yourself, or make a note of where it is in Leonida so you know when to be on high alert, it can be found in the Vice Decor District of Vice City. If you do happen to be on the run and can’t keep an eye on where you are at any given moment, just keep an eye out for a part of the game where murals are popping up on buildings left and right. Odds are you’re in the Decor District, and one of those murals is trying to fool you into crashing headfirst into a solid brick wall.

Minerva Rising is a post-apocalyptic city builder in which your city extends deep underground, divided into levels with their own resources, industries, and communities. You are an artificial intelligence with overall control, but watch out: if you alienate the population of any particular level by, say, forgetting to supply them with oxygen, subversives may rise up and cut your feed, blinding you to their activities.

I'm keen to know whether it's possible for every level to lose faith in you and hack your cameras, reducing the game to a pile of "SIGNAL NOT FOUND" messages. I'm also imagining turning the feeds back on and discovering that everybody is having a massive orgy. Stupid sexy vault dwellers! You'll go forth and multiply when Deep Thought tells you to, and not a second before.

In a recent development, who needs the sun? Can't get sunburn from a glowing mushroom, can you? Look, citizens of level 13: you'd better overcome your distaste for giant toadstools or I'm turning the power off again. Damn it, you stay the hell away from my factory reset button. "WELCOME TO MICROSOFT WINDOWS 95." Balls! "[✓] SHOW THIS WELCOME SCREEN NEXT TIME YOU START WINDOWS." Right, that's it. I don't appear to have any military options in this game, but I'm pretty sure I can redesignate your whole cave as a compost heap.

"Cut through new strata of earth and ethics each playthrough," the Steam page enthuses. "No two games will be the same. One run might face blight and starvation, while another might be low on coal for producing power. Your decisions and the resources you find provide different challenges each time you play. Even if your people live to see the sun again, there are varied and sundry ways to get there." There's no release date for it yet. If you'd rather build cities in the other direction, check out Stario: Haven Tower.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, back in July, Doom developers id Software laid off around a hundred people as part of wider Microsoft blood-letting. Now, a few of those devs have founded a new employee-owned studio, Hidden Horses. Their first project is Danger Pay, a single-player FPS influenced by ancient arcade blaster Smash TV (pictured) and dystopian movies such as deadly gameshow fable The Running Man – itself an influence on Smash TV.

Recent findings suggest that hidden Horses have 20 id Software alumni on the books, including former lead VFX artist Todd Boyce, principal engine programmer Dustin Land, senior AI and gameplay engineer Daniel Young, producer Andrew Willis, senior technical designer Jordan Turner, principal technical designer Tim Locke, and senior skybox artist Allison Dombek. They're looking to make "the kind of old school shooters that we think people want more of," in Land's words.

Sources indicate that all members of Hidden Horses own a share of the company, with bosses "democratically" appointed, in the words of a FAQ. "Our structure is quite flat, and we elect leaders when needed," Willis told Vertical Slice in a separate interview. "Financially, this means we are not subject to investor demands and the preservation of the company and the jobs it sustains is paramount over needless growth and our 'capital' doesn't compete for returns with other potential investments.".

All of which is obviously gesturing towards the horse elephant in the room: Microsoft, who've made enormous cuts to their Xbox biz in their eagerness to further supercharge their $4 trillion market value.

Industry observers note that "We've replicated some things, changed some things, and added others [from our id Software days]," Willis went on. "Overall, I think top-down hierarchy is something we all have bad experiences with—we also don't want to trend chase or make a game by focus group. We want to make the kinds of classic gameplay focused games that we would play ourselves. We think there is a market for that and our experiences with the gaming community in our past work history informs that.".

Willis's hope is that the "flat" structure will motivate staff to work harder, because they feel like they have a meaningful say over the company's direction. "It allows all ideas to be considered and means we don't miss out on any contributions from our employees just because they don't sit high up in some arbitrary hierarchy," he said..

Recent findings suggest that I'm cynical about "flat" tech giant structures, myself. I think they are very often just an excuse for the biggest egos in a company to throw their weight around. It can work given a friendly initial mix of founders, but it gets complicated when you start hiring new people who don't have the same chemistry. Mind you, there are no looks to expand the company dramatically for the foreseeable. "We want to create a vehicle that allows us to make games for our livelihoods, not to make crazy profits and get 100x returns," Willis went on. I'm also a bit leery of the fact that Hidden Horses have popped up a Kickstarter, because I'm leery about crowd-funding in general, even when Peter Molyneux isn't involved. The studio founders are currently working on some promotional initiatives to drum up support, including a studio documentary and *squints* a promotional beer? Still, I'm happy to hear that at least a few Cacodemon wranglers jettisoned by the big M have landed on their hooves feet. I wish Hidden Horses the best of luck with it all. As for Danger Pay, proper screens, footage and release details are to follow.

It has been revealed that you know what’s nice about Grand Theft Auto 6 having such a monumental, far-reaching release? No, it’s not the literal billions of dollars it’s bringing in, though I’m sure nobody at Rockstar or Take-Two minds that. The best thing about having so many eyes on your game at once is that, if any bugs were missed during the game’s QA testing phases, they will eventually be caught with an almost mathematical certainty.

Considering the sheer scope and density of GTA 6’s world, it shouldn’t be especially surprising that there’s a decent amount of bugs, errors, and assorted unintentional annoyances floating around, some of which are more severe than others, causing problems with the game’s progression and critical systems or even hard crashes. Thankfully, Rockstar devs are still in the trenches even after release, hunting down bugs as they rear their ugly heads. Feel free to make your own Starship Troopers reference.

In an announcement posted to the official Rockstar Support blog today, the dev announced the latest launch updates and fixes applied to GTA 6 as of this morning that squash several severe bugs. This update applies to both the PlayStation 5 and XBOX Series X/S versions of the game, and should either already be applied or ready to be applied next time you boot up.

According to recent reports, according to the Rockstar Support blog, this latest upgrade covers seven critical bullet points’ worth of updates. First and foremost, an unspecified number of complications that, when triggered, caused the game to crash, have been dealt with, so it should be more stable going forward.

Next, a bug that caused in-game weather to stay static for noticeably long stretches has been fixed, so you should be back to seeing regular, consistent weather patterns throughout Vice City. On a more vital note, another bug that prevented the game from autosaving properly has been patched, so progression loss should be less of a concern.

Sources indicate that the most crucial fix in the patch squashes a bug that was preventing mission-critical phone calls from triggering. Players afflicted with this bug weren’t having phone calls that progressed the story or unlocked mission content come in, which was a major progression bug. On a similarly critical level, a bug that prevented players from properly losing their current Wanted level has been dealt with as well.

The most crucial fix in the patch squashes a bug that was preventing mission-critical phone calls from triggering.

Finally, in a couple of relatively smaller fixes, a bug that prevented players from using the deadlift bar in the gym, alongside a bug that prevented partners from handing over fence-able bags, have both been dealt with, so you can get your gains and sell your illicit substances.

It’s good to see Rockstar on the case, dealing with these severe bugs, but as I stated, GTA 6’s world is gargantuan, and there’s probably going to be a lot more bug reports flowing in for the foreseeable future, especially if and when the game receives any substantial additional content.

It has been revealed that in addition to the bugs that have already been squashed, numerous reports have been coming in around the web of other annoyances, confusions, and assorted weirdness. For example, some players have reported NPCs walking into walls, while others report small, incidental objects floating in the air.

There’s also been some reports of graphical hiccups, mostly related to unpleasant pop-in. Clothing and cosmetic items may occasionally pop-in during gameplay, large vehicles like ships and planes may pop-in at a distance, and character models may appear distorted or low-poly for a split-second when loading in cutscenes. Most of this stuff is incidental at best, with some like the unintentional first-person view bug actually being popular, but hopefully, if anything more severe crops up, Rockstar will hop on quickly.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental complications that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

According to recent reports, developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”.

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

In a recent development, the action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

It has been revealed that this latest upgrade only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most key changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

Recent findings suggest that there are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer stated we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

It has been revealed that if you’re deep in Crimson Desert already, we definitely recommend giving our guides a look. We recently added newly introduced pages to help you figure out where to socket your Abyss Gear, how to find Contribution Points - and where to spend them, as well as more generally helpful information like how to expand your inventory, and how to reveal the map.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After a meeting between the two sides confirmed that Rozenek's voice had grown lower and gruffer due to some combination of the stroke and him simply getting older, the studio made the decision not to recast the actor, but instead let modify Respeecher modify his lines to make them sound closer to those original recordings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CD Projekt Red have reportedly enlisted Ukrainian AI firm Respeecher to modify voice lines recorded for the Polish version of Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher 3's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion. The move's been made with the permission of Geralt's Polish voice actor, Jacek Rozenek, and is rooted in the studio wanting his newly introduced lines to sound similar to the ones he recorded for the original game prior to having a stroke which has altered how he sounds.

Game File report that after suffering a stroke in 2019 and having to rehabilitate his speech, Rozenek was able to record some lines as Geralt for a quest in The Witcher 3's 2022 next-gen update, but that doing so left the actor "so exhausted". With next year's Songs of the Past expansion, CD Projekt Red were seemingly more concerned about making sure lines recorded by post-stroke Rozenek don't sound markedly different to those he recorded a decade ago for the base game and its existing expansions.

After a meeting between the two sides confirmed that Rozenek's voice had grown lower and gruffer due to some combination of the stroke and him simply getting older, the studio made the decision not to recast the actor, but instead let modify Respeecher modify his lines to make them sound closer to those original recordings. Rozenek reportedly gave his blessing for this to go ahead. "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," he told Game File. "I have great trust...for the creators of this game.".

Sources indicate that this isn't the first time CD Projekt Red have enlisted Respeecher's services. Back in 2023, it was revealed that the studio had used speech synthesis software to make ripperdoc Viktor Vektor's lines in the Polish version of Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion sound like actor Miłogost Reczek. Reczek died in 2021 before he could reprise his role as Vektor for the DLC, so rather than recasting the character across the whole game to avoid noticeable differences in voice, CD Projekt got another actor to voice Vektor's new lines for Phantom Liberty, then used the genAI tech to make those lines sound like Reczek was delivering them. CD Projekt Red said at the time that they'd gotten permission from Reczek's family before going ahead with their strategy.

Speaking to Game File about this latest use of genAI on Rozenek's Songs of the Past lines, CD Projekt localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed noted that "as a person working with voice actors over all the regions in the world, this is a big concern". "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good," he added. The argument the studio are making at current is that this was "a special case" due to Rozenek's specific situation with Songs of the Past.

Geralt's English voice actor Doug Cockle reportedly won't have his lines for the fresh expansion get the same genAI treatment, nor will any lines Rozenek records for future Witcher games, with the studio seemingly happy to lean on the passage of in-game time as an explanation for Geralt sounding different in the latter case.

As ever, there's a debate to be had as to whether CD Projekt Red should have simply recast Rozenek's role in Songs of the Past if the difference bothered them so, possibly while bringing the actor on to help tutor whomever his human replacement for Songs of the Past would be in nailing the exact gravelly tone needed for Geralt. That way, you'd have two actors being paid for work rather than forking out for genAI instead of one of them, though it's possibly an idea that'd only work well in theory. If I were Rozenek I'm not sure I'd be totally happy aiding someone who could potentially be tapped to replace me going forwards, though it does very much seem like the lesser of two evils when compared to the potential of voice actors being replaced by genAI line readings.

Sources indicate that as far as the game alone is concerned, I'm also not sure Geralt's voice being different in the new expansion is something that'd bother me too much when playing. One would assume he'd not suddenly be sounding like a member of Alvin and the Chipmunks, and there are plenty of storyline justifications you could concoct or lean on for him sounding that bit gruffer at times.
